extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning elementary kinematics / geometry of motion
extracted.subtask_description: How to represent and measure motion geometrically: constructing maps, time-charts, hodographs, and curvature-charts to define and compute displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, and curvature. Focuses on graphical procedures, limiting (instantaneous) concepts, and how to interpret chord/tangent slopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical addition of steps (displacements)
rubrics_metrics.description: O'O + OP6 = O'P6 — stepping from O' by O'O then by OP6 reaches the same final spot as a single directed step O'P6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put into words: Step from O' the directed step O'O, then take directed step OP6; the final spot equals taking O'P6 from O'. Caution: do not confuse this geometrical addition with ordinary arithmetical addition (vector addition differs from scalar arithmetic unless motion constrained to one line).

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition by the parallelogram law
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the parallelogram on two steps, and its diagonal will measure a single step equivalent to the sum of the other two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct lines parallel to the two steps to form a parallelogram; the diagonal joining opposite angles represents the geometric sum. This is the practical rule for adding displacements/velocities/accelerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat displacements/velocities/accelerations as steps obeying parallelogram law
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps by which we measure relative position, displacements, velocities, and accelerations obey the parallelogram law — they are added geometrically, not arithmetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All kinematic conceptions (displacement, velocity, spin, acceleration) can be represented as directed steps; additions and combinations must be performed geometrically (vector addition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a time-chart (geometrical time-table)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot stations (positions) down a vertical axis proportionally to distance and plot times along a horizontal axis proportionally to minutes; join corresponding intersections to obtain points Q1,Q2,... and draw a continuous curve (the time-chart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scales (e.g., eighths of an inch per furlong, x/ths per minute) so vertical units represent distance and horizontal units represent time; to find position at a given time scale off horizontally to the curve and project to the distance axis; conversely, read time for a given position. Time-chart conveys more information than a simple timetable column.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-chart as full description (map + time-chart)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taken with a map of the path, the time-chart fully describes a point-motion: map gives path geometry, time-chart gives position as function of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental problem is to ascertain the map and the time-chart; the time-chart allows determining position at each instant and time to reach any position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope as measure of steepness for straight lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The slope of a straight line is the vertical rise per unit horizontal distance (e.g., 20 feet rise in 100 feet run = slope 1/5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slope is a fitting measure of steepness: number of vertical units risen for one horizontal unit. Use basic proportionality/triangle similarity to justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean slope of a curved portion via chord
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curved line segment AC, the slope of the chord AC is the mean slope of the portion — the uniform average slope that would give the same net rise over the horizontal distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although local steepness may vary, the chord gives the average (mean) steepness over that finite interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope of the tangent as steepness at a point (limit / instantaneous)
rubrics_metrics.description: By moving the chord's endpoint toward the point A, the limiting straight line (tangent) measures the steepness of the curve at A; the slope of the tangent is the measure of steepness at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses the limiting process: mean for a vanishingly small segment gives the instantaneous steepness (an ideal limit not attained in perception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed as slope of the time-chart (mean and instantaneous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean speed over an interval is the slope of the corresponding chord on the time-chart (miles per minute); instantaneous (actual) speed at an instant is the slope of the tangent to the time-chart at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary the chord length: shorter chords give different mean speeds; the limit as chord length → 0 gives instantaneous speed. Speed unit is space unit per time unit (e.g., miles per minute). If time-chart is straight, speed is uniform; otherwise variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity as combination of speed and bearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocity = speed (magnitude) + bearing (direction and sense); representable by a directed step whose length measures speed and direction shows bearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To fully describe velocity at position P, combine slope of tangent (speed) with direction of tangent (bearing) and the sense along the tangent (e.g., from P6 to P7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the velocity diagram (hodograph)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a pole I draw rays IV1, IV2, ... parallel to the tangents at successive points of the path, and on each ray measure off a length equal to the speed at that point; the locus of the endpoints V1,V2,... is the hodograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hodograph is a diagram of velocities: its rays give velocities of P relative to O; plotted densely, points approach a continuous curve. It summarizes changes in magnitude and direction of motion and can be constructed from the map and time-chart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration as change of velocity (velocity of V on hodograph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: if V moves along the hodograph then V's velocity (i.e., the velocity of V along its curve) measures how P's velocity changes; this is the acceleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may construct a hodograph of the hodograph (acceleration-diagram). Acceleration stands in the same relation to velocity as velocity does to position-step; acceleration can be represented by steps (directed increments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of acceleration into spurt and shunt
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceleration consists of (i) a spurt (change in magnitude: speed increased or decreased) and (ii) a shunt (change in bearing: direction turned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: train quickens from 40 to 60 mph (spurt) while changing heading from north to north-east (shunt). Spurt can be negative (retardation). Acceleration is the combined effect of spurting and shunting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean acceleration as mean spurt + mean shunt
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean spurt = increase of speed per unit time (difference in lengths IV5–IV4 divided by time); mean shunt = increase of angle per unit time (angle turned divided by time); the mean acceleration is the combined mean rate of spurting and shunting over the interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent mean acceleration by the step V4V5 added in the given time interval (parallelogram-law addition). Comparing maps shows correspondence between adding position-steps and adding velocity-steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantaneous acceleration via tangent to hodograph / limiting process
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual (instantaneous) acceleration appears as the velocity of V along the hodograph: the instantaneous change in IV at V4 is along the hodograph tangent and measured by its slope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either view acceleration as velocity of V or as combined instantaneous stretch (spurt) and spin (shunt) of IV; both equivalent. The increment V4V5 is to be added geometrically (parallelogram law), however small in conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean curvature as angle turned per unit arc length; actual curvature as limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean curvature of a curve element P4P5 is the ratio of the angle through which the tangent turns (L4NL5) to the length of the element P4P5 (average turn per unit length). Actual curvature is the limit of mean curvature as the element length vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mean curvature measures total bending over a finite segment; take the limit to get instantaneous curvature. Ensure the small arc has no change of sense of bending (take sufficiently small element).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and use of the curvature-chart to measure curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot units of angle along a horizontal axis and points along a vertical axis (similar to time-chart construction), form points Q2,Q3,... and join to get a curvature-chart; the slope of a chord in this chart (to the vertical) measures the mean curvature of the corresponding portion of the original curve, and the slope of its tangent gives the actual curvature at a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose angular units (circular measure, radians) and use the standard circle of unit radius to relate arc and angle; as chord Q4Q5 shortens, mean curvature approaches actual curvature; the slope of tangent in curvature-chart is a measurable quantity for each point.
